summary.title: The Ten Commandments of Egoless Programming
summary.one_liner: Ten interpersonal rules for software developers, drawn from Jerry Weinberg's 1971 book The Psychology of Computer Programming, for taking feedback and code review without ego.
takeaways: Expect to make mistakes and treat code review as a way to find them early rather than a personal attack.
Separate yourself from your code: critique the code, not the coder, and keep comments positive and tied to standards or specs.
Respect and authority come from knowledge, so keep learning and stay open to input from others.
Discuss stylistic rewrites within a review instead of changing others' code alone, and accept being overruled gracefully.
Stay open, collaborative and patient with less technical colleagues, avoiding the 'guy in the room' isolation.
summary.summary: This Coding Horror blog post reproduces the ten principles of egoless programming originally set out by Jerry Weinberg in The Psychology of Computer Programming (1971). Each commandment is a short paragraph covering mistakes, code review, humility, rewriting code, respect for non-technical colleagues, handling change, earning authority through knowledge, accepting defeat, avoiding isolation, and giving kind, code-focused criticism. The post is a brief list with no code or technical implementation details, and it closes by noting the principles remain timeless.
